analysis.one_liner: Protects millions of acres of Utah red rock desert as wilderness, banning new mining and drilling there.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 160 cosponsors, including 8 Republicans, but never received a vote in the House before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add roughly nine million acres of federal land in Utah — canyon country around Canyonlands, the San Rafael Swell, the Book Cliffs, and the Great Basin — to the National Wilderness Preservation System. Wilderness is the strictest land protection in U.S. law: no new mining claims, no oil, gas, or geothermal leasing, no new roads, and no motorized use, though existing livestock grazing would continue. The bill died in the House Natural Resources Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans who hike, camp, hunt, or value undeveloped public land gain permanent protection for some of the country's most scenic desert. The bill preserves archaeological sites in Cedar Mesa from vandalism, keeps habitat intact for desert bighorn sheep, elk, and bison, and reserves federal water rights for the wilderness areas.

how_it_helps.text: Designates wilderness across ten Utah regions, from the Great Basin to Canyonlands Basin, making the protection permanent unless Congress acts again [S2].
Withdraws the designated land from mining claims and from mineral and geothermal leasing, so companies could not develop it [S3].
Continues existing livestock grazing under reasonable regulation, preserving current ranching use of the land [S3].
Sets specific road setbacks so that popular routes and access points stay open, rather than closing land wholesale [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mining, oil and gas, and geothermal companies lose the ability to stake claims or lease the designated federal land. Off-road vehicle users lose areas open to motorized travel. The public forgoes whatever energy and mineral revenue those lands could have produced.

drawbacks.text: The bill withdraws the land from all mining and mineral and geothermal leasing, permanently forgoing resource development on millions of acres [S3].
Wilderness designation bans motorized and mechanized travel, so off-road vehicle riders lose access to areas they currently use [S3].
Designation is permanent; future Congresses could not easily open the land even if energy needs or local preferences change [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is permanent and covers some of the largest undisturbed desert landscapes in the lower 48 states, which is a real and lasting gain for the public. The cost is forgone energy and mineral development and reduced motorized access, which opponents — especially Utah's delegation and extractive industries — considered too high. The bill was drafted to soften the blow by keeping grazing and existing roads, but it offered nothing to industries that wanted to develop the land.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its public lands subcommittee, sat there for the rest of the two-year Congress, and never came up for a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 18, 2007 with 160 original cosponsors and referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources [S5].
It gathered 160 cosponsors total, 152 Democrats and 8 Republicans [S4].
On May 18, 2007 it was referred to the Subcommittee on National Parks, Forests and Public Lands, and no further action was taken before the Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mining, oil and gas, and geothermal interests kept their access to Utah's red rock country, since no protections were enacted and the land remained open to leasing and claims.

for.name: Rep. Maurice Hinchey
for.role: Sponsor, House Natural Resources Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 160 cosponsors for it [S4].

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or floor vote on the bill; after initial referral it moved only to a subcommittee and stayed there [S5].

against.name: Utah's congressional delegation
against.role: Senators and House members from Utah
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill throughout this era, arguing it would lock up Utah land against local interests and block energy development; no Utah member cosponsored it [S4].

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 152 of 160 cosponsors were Democrats, with 8 Republicans joining — and the bill died in committee without a recorded vote.

industries.industry: Mining, oil and gas, and geothermal companies
industries.note: The bill withdraws designated land from mining claims and mineral and geothermal leasing, ending potential development there. Its interest in keeping the land open runs directly against the public's interest in permanent protection.
Permanent wilderness protection preserves the scenic landscapes that draw hikers, hunters, and tourists to Utah's canyon country. The same land stays open for quiet recreation forever.
The bill explicitly permits existing livestock grazing to continue within the new wilderness areas. Ranchers keep their current use of the land even under strict protection.
Wilderness bans motorized travel, closing areas now open to off-road vehicles. The industry's interest in keeping land open to machines conflicts with wilderness protection.
